items.statement: An updated rapid review will find that wearable activity feedback after knee replacement increases daily steps at about three months but produces no patient-important improvement in function (standardised mean difference below 0.2).
items.rationale: Need and practice change are high because a lease decision depends on the answer; novelty is low because it updates an existing review; feasibility and parsimony are high because one primary outcome can be updated in eight weeks.
items.risks: Few new trials since 2022; heterogeneous function scales; industry-funded trials.

items.statement: Benefits on function and adherence are smaller in patients aged 75 or over and in patients without a smartphone.
items.rationale: Matters for a centre where a third of patients are over 75, but few trials report subgroups, so it will be described rather than tested.
items.risks: Ecological reasoning from trials that excluded the oldest patients.

items.statement: Feedback that includes messages from a named physiotherapist improves function more than automated step targets alone.
items.rationale: Patients describe named messages as what kept them walking, but head-to-head comparisons are unlikely to exist.
items.risks: Comparison across trials confounded by other trial differences.

summary: Three hypotheses; h1 selected because it answers the committee's question with one primary outcome.
